prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "BANK OF NOVA SCOTIA" (ticker BNS), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "BNS", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: The Bank of Nova Scotia
markets: Canadian personal and commercial banking (accounts, mortgages, credit cards, auto loans, Tangerine digital bank)
International banking in Mexico, Chile, Peru, the Caribbean and Central America
Wealth management and asset management (Scotia Wealth Management, ScotiaMcLeod, Dynamic Funds, Jarislowsky Fraser)
Capital markets and corporate banking (Scotiabank Global Banking and Markets) across the Americas

mission.source: Scotiabank's stated purpose, published in its Q4 2025 Investor Factsheet and annual report
mission.plain: Scotiabank says it exists to help its clients, their families and communities build a better future.

about.plain: Scotiabank is one of Canada's five big banks. It keeps people's money safe, lends money for homes, cars and businesses, and gives out credit cards. It is also a big bank in Mexico, Chile, Peru and the Caribbean, and it helps people invest and helps large companies raise money. It earns money from the gap between what it pays savers and what it charges borrowers, plus fees.
about.customers: More than 11 million Canadian banking customers, over 8 million international banking clients, plus wealth clients, companies and governments.
about.everyday: Many Canadians earn Scene+ points with Scotiabank cards when they shop at Sobeys or go to Cineplex movies, and Tangerine, its online bank, is its own brand.

money.plain: Bank accounts, mortgages, credit cards and business loans in Canada, including Tangerine
Banking for people and businesses in Mexico, Chile, Peru and the Caribbean
Investment advice, mutual funds and brokerage accounts
Loans, trading and deal advice for big companies and governments
A 14.9% ownership stake in a large US regional bank

result.summary: Scotiabank has a real but middling moat: it is one of Canada's five big banks in a protected, concentrated market, with sticky deposits, its Scene+ loyalty program and AA-range credit ratings. But it earns lower returns than RBC and TD (FY2025 reported ROE 9.7%), ranked last among the Big Five in J.D. Power's 2025 Canadian satisfaction study, and its Latin American franchise competes against strong local leaders, so the advantage is narrower than its biggest Canadian peers'.

pricingPower.evidence: Canada's concentrated banking market lets Scotiabank widen spreads: its net interest margin rose to 2.49% in Q3 2026 from 2.36% a year earlier and nine-month FY2026 revenue rose 7.4% to C$30,018M while adjusted expenses grew 4.7%; but loan and deposit pricing follows central-bank rates and it ranked last of the Big Five (595 points) in J.D. Power's 2025 satisfaction study.

moats.evidence: Scotiabank is a 190-year-old household name in Canada and much of Latin America with senior debt rated Aa2/AA (Moody's/Fitch), but its brand trails RBC and TD in customer satisfaction.
Payroll accounts, mortgages, credit cards and Scene+ points make clients slow to move, which keeps a large base of low-cost deposits (C$1,006,015M at July 31, 2026).
Scene+, co-owned with Empire and Cineplex, has over 15 million members and added Shell as a partner in 2026, giving a modest loyalty network effect around its cards.
With C$1.55 trillion of assets it spreads technology and compliance costs widely, but its Q3 2026 productivity ratio of 52.7% is only middling among Canadian banks.
Canada's banking market is dominated by six large banks protected by OSFI regulation and the federal widely-held ownership rules, limiting new entrants.
Scotiabank is an incumbent universal bank; its Tangerine digital bank is a defensive offshoot rather than a model rivals cannot copy.
It has long experience running banks across the Pacific Alliance countries and the Caribbean, but its risk and operating processes have not produced superior returns.
Federal banking licences and its 14.9% KeyCorp stake are valuable, but no exclusive asset sets it clearly apart from Canadian peers.

customers.evidence: Scotiabank scored 595 in J.D. Power's 2025 Canada Retail Banking Satisfaction Study, last among the Big Five (average 604), while its own Tangerine Bank ranked first of all banks with 683; Scene+ has over 15 million members.

talent.evidence: Scotiabank was named one of Canada's Top 100 Employers for 2026 and ranked #40 among Great Place to Work's 2026 Best Workplaces in Canada (1,000+ employees), but it cut staff (FTEs 81,734 at July 31, 2026 vs 87,317 a year earlier) and took a C$373M restructuring charge in Q4 2025.

product.evidence: Its products are standard banking products; Euromoney named it Canada's best bank in its 2024 Awards for Excellence and Tangerine and Scene+ cards stand out, but Scotiabank's main brand ranks last among the Big Five in J.D. Power customer satisfaction.

threats: Credit losses in Canada and Latin America: PCL was C$3,472M in nine-month FY2026 as mortgage renewals at higher rates and consumer stress weigh on borrowers

Political, currency and economic volatility in Mexico, Chile, Peru and the Caribbean

Execution risk on its strategic pivot to North America, including the KeyCorp stake and the 20.3% Davivienda stake received for its Colombia, Costa Rica and Panama banks
Weaker customer satisfaction than Big Five peers (last in J.D. Power's 2025 study) limiting cross-selling

ceo.name: Scott Thomson
ceo.background: Former CEO of Finning International, CFO of Talisman Energy, EVP Corporate Development at BCE and Goldman Sachs banker; BA in economics and political science from Queen's University and MBA from the University of Chicago

c1.evidence: Scotiabank is a leader in Canadian and Latin American banking, mature industries rather than emerging, fast-growing ones.

c2.evidence: Clients choose Scotiabank for convenience, its branch network (1,984 branches and offices), Scene+ rewards and its Latin American footprint, and Canada's concentrated market makes that durable, but its products are similar to rivals' and its satisfaction scores trail peers.

c3.evidence: Most Canadians and many Latin Americans know the Scotiabank name and it is one of Canada's Big Five, but it is not the default leader and ranked last of the Big Five in J.D. Power's 2025 satisfaction study.

c4.evidence: Its purpose 'for every future' appears in investor materials, but management's public focus is on financial targets such as its 14%+ ROE objective and reallocating capital to North America.

c6.evidence: “big Canadian bank, Latin America, Scene+ points, dividend payer”: people see Scotiabank as a solid, international Canadian bank, a mostly neutral-to-positive impression tempered by weaker customer service scores than peers.

c7.evidence: Banking in Canada, Mexico and the Andean countries is huge and grows with the economy, but it is not riding a fast secular trend like AI or cloud.

c8.evidence: It is expanding in the US through its 14.9% KeyCorp stake and in Mexico, but its name and model tie it to traditional banking.

m1.evidence: Thomson set out a clear plan at the December 2023 Investor Day to reallocate capital to North America and earn primary client relationships, which he has executed, but it is a restructuring plan rather than a bold vision of the future.

m2.evidence: Thomson is a professional manager who joined the bank as an outsider in 2022 and is reshaping it for the long term, but he is not a founder.

m4.evidence: He emphasises 'earning primary client relationships' and 'winning as one team', but there is little public evidence of exceptional servant leadership, and the bank cut thousands of jobs in 2025.

m5.evidence: Scotiabank's culture is that of a large, conservative bank focused on simplification and cost control rather than inventing new products.

m6.evidence: Thomson's background is in finance and industrial management (Goldman Sachs, BCE, Talisman, Finning), not engineering or technology.

m7.evidence: Thomson has no known integrity issues and runs a bank that has paid dividends continuously since 1833, but his stewardship is aimed mainly at shareholder returns.

m7b.evidence: No record found of Scott Thomson giving a commencement speech at Stanford, Harvard, MIT or a similar top university.

m8b.evidence: Thomson has a measured, low-key banker's public persona.

m9.evidence: Under Thomson adjusted ROE rose to 14.2% in Q3 2026 (above the 14% target) from 11.8% in FY2025, Q3 2026 net income hit a record C$2,953M, and he completed the KeyCorp investment and the Colombia, Costa Rica and Panama exit.

m10.evidence: Scotiabank is not known for frugality, though it cut full-time staff to 81,734 at July 31, 2026 from 87,317 a year earlier and took a C$373M restructuring charge in Q4 2025.

c10.evidence: Scotiabank keeps savings safe and funds homes and businesses for more than 20 million clients across the Americas, important but ordinary financial services.

p2.evidence: Running a safe, regulated multinational bank is hard and important, but many banks do it and the products are not technologically unique.

f1.evidence: Revenue rose in four of the last five years, from C$31,336M in FY2020 to C$37,741M in FY2025, after a small dip to C$31,252M in FY2021.

f2.evidence: Pre-tax margin fell from 41.0% of revenue in FY2021 (C$12,826M) to 27.8% in FY2025 (C$10,509M) as credit losses and expenses, including a C$1,422M impairment, rose.

f3.evidence: Shareholders' equity was C$90,622M at July 31, 2026 and subordinated debentures only C$6,919M against C$62,455M of cash and deposits with banks, but as a bank it is highly leveraged, with liabilities about 16x equity.

f4.evidence: Income before taxes fell from C$12,932M in FY2022 to C$10,509M in FY2025, and operating cash flow swung from C$15,652M in FY2024 to C$5,407M in FY2025.

v1.evidence: Scotiabank's banking products are not clearly best in class; RBC leads the Big Five in J.D. Power satisfaction while Scotiabank ranks last.

v2.evidence: Scotiabank was named one of Canada's Top 100 Employers for 2026 and #40 in Great Place to Work's 2026 Best Workplaces in Canada (1,000+ employees), but it is not seen as one of the very best places to work.

c5.evidence: Its loans and accounts help millions of families and businesses in Canada and Latin America, but if it disappeared other banks would quickly absorb its clients.
